(p-3) **Surat al-Naba' (The Tidings)**
It is also called **Surat al-Tasa'ul (The Questioning)**.
It is entirely Meccan, by consensus.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ Its original form is *ʿan mā*, so the nūn was assimilated into the mīm, and the alif of *mā* was dropped, as in their saying *fīm* and *bim*. The exegetes said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, the polytheists began asking one another, saying, "What is it that he has brought?" They argued and disputed about what he had been sent with, and so this verse was revealed. The wording is that of a question, but the meaning is to magnify the matter, as they say, "What is Zayd?" when you wish to glorify his station. Then He explained what they were asking about, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿about the great tidings﴾, meaning, about the news of great importance. On this there are three views.

The first: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid, Muqatil, and al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: "When He answered, *ʿamma* became as if it meant: 'For what reason are they asking about the Qur'an?'"
The second: it is the Resurrection. This was said by Qatada.
The third: it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), related by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in which they are in disagreement﴾. For one who says it is the Qur'an, the disagreement is that the polytheists differed about it: some said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, and some said it is "the fables of the ancients," and so on. Likewise for one who says it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ). As for one who says it is the Resurrection and the Last Day, there are two views on their disagreement about it.
One: they disagreed about it when they heard of it; some of them affirmed and believed, and some denied. This is the meaning of Qatada's statement.
Two: the Muslims and the polytheists disagreed about it, the Muslims affirmed it and the polytheists denied it. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay!﴾ Some said it is a rebuke and a warning. Others said it is a negation of their disagreement, meaning: the matter is not as they say. ﴿They will come to know﴾ the outcome of their denial when the matter becomes clear. ﴿Again, nay! They will come to know﴾: a warning upon a warning. Ibn ʿAmir read *sa-ta-ʿlamūn* with the tā' in both places.

Then He mentioned His handiwork so that they might recognize His oneness, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place﴾, that is, a bed and a carpet, ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ for the earth, so that it would not sway. ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾, that is, in kinds and opposites: males and females, black and white and red. ﴿And We made your sleep a repose﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: that is, a rest for your bodies. We have explained this in [al-Furqan: 47], and we explained there His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the night a covering﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the day a means of livelihood﴾, that is, a cause of your livelihood. *Maʿāsh* means subsistence, and everything by which one lives is a *maʿāsh*. The meaning is: We made the day a time for seeking livelihood. Ibn Qutayba said: *maʿāsh* means *ʿaysh* (living), and it is a verbal noun. ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾. Muqatil said: these are the heavens, the thickness of each heaven being a five-hundred-year journey, and between every two heavens is the same distance, and they are above you, O children of Adam. So beware lest you disobey, for [they] would fall upon you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made a lamp, blazing﴾, meaning the sun. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *wahhāj* is the bright one. The philologists said: *al-Wahhāj* is the blazing one. It was also said: *al-Wahhāj* combines light and heat.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the *muʿṣirāt*﴾. On this there are three views.
One: they are the heavens. This was said by Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jubayr.
Two: they are the winds. This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Ikrima, Qatada, and Muqatil also said so. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are the south winds. According to this view, *min* means *bi* (with), so the sense is: *bi-l-muʿṣirāt* (by means of the *muʿṣirāt*). The winds were called *muʿṣirāt* because they draw out the rain.
Three: they are the clouds. This was related by al-Walibi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Rabiʿ also said so. Al-Farra' said: the cloud *muʿṣir* is one that is dripping with rain but has not yet gathered, like the girl *muʿṣir* who is almost reaching menstruation but has not yet menstruated. Ibn Qutayba likewise said: clouds were likened to young girls approaching puberty, and *muʿṣir* is a girl who has come close to menstruation. Al-Zajjaj said: the clouds were called *muʿṣirāt* just as it is said, "The crop was harvested (*ajazza*), so it is *mujazz*," meaning it reached the point of being harvested. Likewise the cloud, when it reaches the point of raining, has become *muʿṣir*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿water pouring forth﴾. Muqatil said: that is, abundant rain, poured down, each part following another. Others said: it is said *thajja al-māʾ yathujju*, when water pours out.
﴿That We may bring forth thereby﴾, that is, by that water, ﴿grain and plants﴾. On this there are two views.
One: *ḥabb* is what people eat, and *nabāt* is what the earth produces of what people and cattle eat. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zajjaj said: everything that is harvested is *ḥabb*, and everything that livestock eat of the pasture is *nabāt*.
Two: *ḥabb* is pearl and *nabāt* is grass. Ikrima said: Allah did not send down any drop from the sky without causing pearls to grow in the sea by it, and grass on the land.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and gardens, luxuriant﴾, meaning orchards. Abu ʿUbayda said: that is, intertwined with trees, with no gaps between them. The singular is *laffāʾ*, and *jannāt luff* is the plural, and the plural of the plural is *alfāf*. The exegetes said: by mentioning these created things He pointed to the Resurrection.

Then He informed about the Day of Resurrection, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision﴾, that is, the Day of judgment among creatures, ﴿is an appointed time﴾ for what Allah promised of reward and punishment. ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes﴾, that is, in companies, company after company from every place. ﴿And the sky will be opened﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *wa-futtiḥat* with shaddah. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with lightness. It is opened for the descent of the angels. ﴿And it will become gates﴾, that is, having gates. ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion﴾ from their places, ﴿and they will become a mirage﴾, that is, like a mirage, because they will become scattered dust, so that the observer sees them like a mirage after their firmness and solidity. ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a place of ambush﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: *mirṣād* is a place where they lie in wait, that is, it is prepared for them, and its guardians lie in wait for the disbelievers in it. Al-Azhari said: *al-mirṣād* is the place where the watcher lies in wait for the enemy. Then He explained for whom it is an ambush, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: for the polytheists, that is, a destination.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾. Ḥamzah read *labithīn*, and the meaning in both is one. It is said: "He is *lābith* in the place" and "*labith*." Similar are *ṭāmiʿ* and *ṭamiʿ*, and *fārih* and *farih*. As for *al-aḥqāb*, it is the plural of *ḥiqb*, and we have mentioned the disagreement about it in [al-Kahf: 60].

If it is asked: what is the meaning of mentioning ages, when their dwelling in the Fire has no end? On this there are two answers.
One: this does not indicate a limit, because whenever one age passes, another follows it. Had He said "remaining therein for ten ages or five," it would have indicated a limit. This is the view of Ibn Qutayba and the majority. Its explanation is that the time of the people of Paradise and Hell can be conceived as falling under a count, even though it has no end.
Two: the meaning is that they will remain therein for ages, ﴿tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾ during the ages. As for their dwelling in the Fire, it is eternal. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Its explanation is that the ages are a limit for their punishment with boiling water and *ghassāq*; when the ages have ended, they will be punished with other punishments.
As for the meaning of *bard* (coolness), there are three views.
One: it is the coolness of drink. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: they will not taste therein the coolness of drink, nor drink.
Two: it is rest and comfort. This was said by al-Hasan and ʿAṭāʾ.
Three: it is sleep. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu ʿUbayda, and Ibn Qutayba, and they recited:
*"If I wish, I forbid women other than you, and if I wish, I do not taste cool water (nuqākh) nor sleep (bard)."*
Ibn Qutayba said: *nuqākh* is water, and *bard* is sleep, named so because the heat cools within it. Muqatil said: they will not taste therein any coolness that would benefit them from its heat, nor any drink that would benefit them from thirst. ﴿Except boiling water and *ghassāq*﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *ghasāqan* with lightness. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal, and Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim read it with shaddah.
The mention of *ḥamīm* and *ghassāq* has already preceded [p. 57].

﴿As a fitting recompense﴾. Al-Farra' said: suitable to their deeds. Others said: they are recompensed with a recompense fitting to their deeds, according to its measure. There is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾. On this there are two views.
One: they did not fear being called to account, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by the majority.
Two: they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾. Al-Farra' said: *al-kiddhāb* with shaddah is an eloquent Yemeni dialect. They say: "I denied it *kiddhāban*," and "I tore the shirt *kharrāqan*," and every *faʿaltu* in their dialect has a verbal noun with shaddah. An Arab from among them, while I was at al-Marwah, asked me for a legal ruling: "Is shaving more beloved to you, or cutting short?" And one of the Banu Kilab recited to me:
*"Indeed, it has long kept me away from my companions, and from needs whose fulfillment is my healing."*
As for the people of Najd, they say: "I denied it *takdhīban*." Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-kiddhāb* is stronger than *al-kidhāb*, and both are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual denial). Al-Aʿshā said:
*"So I believed her, and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And everything We have enumerated We have recorded in a book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *kulla* is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose explanation is *aḥṣaynāhu* (We have enumerated it). The meaning is: We enumerated everything. ﴿In a book﴾ is an emphasis on *aḥṣaynāhu*, because the meaning of *aḥṣaynāhu* and *kataknāhu* (We recorded it) is one in what is retained and established. So the meaning is: We recorded it as a book. The exegetes said: every deed was recorded by Us in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ).
﴿So taste! We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ That is, it will be said to them: taste the recompense of your deeds.

﴿Indeed, for the righteous﴾, those who did not associate partners with Allah, ﴿is a place of success﴾. On this there are two views.
One: a place of recreation. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.
Two: they succeeded by being saved from the Fire by Paradise, and from punishment by mercy. This was said by Qatada. Ibn Qutayba said: *mafāzan* is in the place of *fawz* (success).

﴿Gardens﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ḥadāʾiq* are orchards of palm trees; its singular is *ḥadīqah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and maidens of equal age﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-kawāʿib* are those with firm breasts. Ibn Fāris said: it is said, "the woman *kaʿabat* a *kaʿābah*," so she is *kāʿib*, when her breasts protrude. We have mentioned the meaning of *al-atrāb* (of equal age) in [p. 52].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾. On this there are three views.
One: it is full. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd also said so.
Two: it is continuous. This was related by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr also said so. It is also reported from Mujahid as both views.
Three: it is pure. This was said by Ikrima.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, when they drink it, ﴿any idle talk﴾, which we have mentioned in [al-Tur: 23] and elsewhere, ﴿nor any lying﴾, that is, they will not lie to one another, because the people of this world, when they drink wine, speak falsehood, but the people of Paradise are exempt from that.

Al-Farra' said: the reading of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, is *kiḍāban* with lightness, as if—and Allah knows best—they will not lie to one another therein. Al-Kisa'i would read it with lightness, and with shaddah in "They denied Our signs with complete denial (*kiddhāban*)," because "they denied" specifies *kiddhāb* as a verbal noun, whereas here it is not specified by a verb that makes it a verbal noun. We have already mentioned from Abu ʿUbayda that *kiddhāb* with shaddah and with lightness is the verbal noun of *al-mukādhaba*. Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: *kidhāb* with lightness is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, like *kitāb* is the verbal noun of *kataba*.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 78, verses 1–40 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a recompense﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that He recompensed them with that as a recompense, and likewise "a gift" (ʿaṭāʾ), because "He gave them" (aʿṭāhum) and "He recompensed them" (jāzāhum) have one meaning. And ﴿a reckoning﴾ means: what suffices them, i.e., in it is everything they desire. It is said: "Ahsabanī kadhā" (meaning "it sufficed me").

﴿Lord of the heavens﴾: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Mufaḍḍal recited "Rabbu as-samawāti wal-arḍi wa mā baynahumā al-Raḥmānu" with the bāʾ of "Rabb" and the nūn of "al-Raḥmān" in the nominative (rafʿ), meaning: He is the Lord of the heavens. ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir recited with the bāʾ and nūn in the genitive (khafḍ), as an attribute of "your Lord" (rabbika). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī recited with a kasra on the bāʾ and a rafʿ on the nūn. Al-Farrāʾ (a grammarian, the scholar who chose this reading) preferred this reading, and a group agreed with him, giving as the reason that "Rabb" is close to the genitive, while "al-Raḥmān" is further from it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not possess from Him any address﴾. There are two views concerning it:
One: they will not possess intercession except by His permission. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib. The second: creation cannot speak to the Lord except by His permission. This was said by Muqātil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾. Concerning "the Spirit" there are seven views:
The first: that it is one of the soldiers of God, the Exalted, and they are not angels. Ibn ʿAbbās related it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Mujāhid said: they are a creation in the form of the children of Adam, who eat and drink.
The second: that it is an angel greater than the heavens, the mountains and the angels. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Muqātil ibn Sulaymān. ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Spirit is an angel greater than anything God has created. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he alone stands in one row, and all the angels stand in one row, so his size is like their rows."
The third: that they are the spirits of people, who stand with the angels between the two blasts, before they are returned to the bodies. ʿAṭiyyah related it from Ibn ʿAbbās.
The fourth: that it is Jibrīl (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
The fifth: that they are the children of Adam. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.
The sixth: that it is the Qurʾān. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.
The seventh: that they are the noblest of the angels. This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the angels in rows﴾. Al-Shaʿbī said: they are two lines, one line of the Spirit and one line of the angels. On this view the meaning is: the Day the Spirit stands in rows, and the angels in rows. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿ṣaffan﴾ is "in rows" (ṣufūfan).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not speak﴾, meaning all creation, ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ to speak, ﴿and who speaks rightly﴾, i.e., who spoke rightly in the world, and this is the testimony to monotheism according to most exegetes. Mujāhid said: he spoke the truth in the world and acted upon it. ﴿That is the true Day﴾, the one that occurs and befalls without doubt. ﴿So whoever wills, let him take to his Lord a return﴾, i.e., a place of return to Him through obedience to Him.

Then He warned the disbelievers of Makkah, saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day a man will look at what his hands have put forth﴾, i.e., he will see his deed recorded in his book, whether good or bad. ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Oh, I wish I were dust!"﴾, i.e., "I wish I had not been resurrected."

Al-Thaʿlabī related from some of his teachers that he saw in some exegeses that the disbeliever here is Iblīs, because he reproached Adam, since he was created from dust, so on the Day of Resurrection he wished that he had been in the place of Adam, and said: "Oh, I wish I were dust!"

Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *wa-futtiḥat* with shaddah. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with lightness. It is opened for the descent of the angels. ﴿And it will become gates﴾, that is, having gates. ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion﴾ from their places, ﴿and they will become a mirage﴾, that is, like a mirage, because they will become scattered dust, so that the observer sees them like a mirage after their firmness and solidity. ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a place of ambush﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: *mirṣād* is a place where they lie in wait, that is, it is prepared for them, and its guardians lie in wait for the disbelievers in it. Al-Azhari said: *al-mirṣād* is the place where the watcher lies in wait for the enemy. Then He explained for whom it is an ambush, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: for the polytheists, that is, a destination.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾. Ḥamzah read *labithīn*, and the meaning in both is one. It is said: "He is *lābith* in the place" and "*labith*." Similar are *ṭāmiʿ* and *ṭamiʿ*, and *fārih* and *farih*. As for *al-aḥqāb*, it is the plural of *ḥiqb*, and we have mentioned the disagreement about it in [al-Kahf: 60].

If it is asked: what is the meaning of mentioning ages, when their dwelling in the Fire has no end? On this there are two answers.
One: this does not indicate a limit, because whenever one age passes, another follows it. Had He said "remaining therein for ten ages or five," it would have indicated a limit. This is the view of Ibn Qutayba and the majority. Its explanation is that the time of the people of Paradise and Hell can be conceived as falling under a count, even though it has no end.
Two: the meaning is that they will remain therein for ages, ﴿tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾ during the ages. As for their dwelling in the Fire, it is eternal. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Its explanation is that the ages are a limit for their punishment with boiling water and *ghassāq*; when the ages have ended, they will be punished with other punishments.
As for the meaning of *bard* (coolness), there are three views.
One: it is the coolness of drink. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: they will not taste therein the coolness of drink, nor drink.
Two: it is rest and comfort. This was said by al-Hasan and ʿAṭāʾ.
Three: it is sleep. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu ʿUbayda, and Ibn Qutayba, and they recited:
*"If I wish, I forbid women other than you, and if I wish, I do not taste cool water (nuqākh) nor sleep (bard)."*
Ibn Qutayba said: *nuqākh* is water, and *bard* is sleep, named so because the heat cools within it. Muqatil said: they will not taste therein any coolness that would benefit them from its heat, nor any drink that would benefit them from thirst. ﴿Except boiling water and *ghassāq*﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *ghasāqan* with lightness. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal, and Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim read it with shaddah.
The mention of *ḥamīm* and *ghassāq* has already preceded [p. 57].

﴿As a fitting recompense﴾. Al-Farra' said: suitable to their deeds. Others said: they are recompensed with a recompense fitting to their deeds, according to its measure. There is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾. On this there are two views.
One: they did not fear being called to account, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by the majority.
Two: they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾. Al-Farra' said: *al-kiddhāb* with shaddah is an eloquent Yemeni dialect. They say: "I denied it *kiddhāban*," and "I tore the shirt *kharrāqan*," and every *faʿaltu* in their dialect has a verbal noun with shaddah. An Arab from among them, while I was at al-Marwah, asked me for a legal ruling: "Is shaving more beloved to you, or cutting short?" And one of the Banu Kilab recited to me:
*"Indeed, it has long kept me away from my companions, and from needs whose fulfillment is my healing."*
As for the people of Najd, they say: "I denied it *takdhīban*." Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-kiddhāb* is stronger than *al-kidhāb*, and both are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual denial). Al-Aʿshā said:
*"So I believed her, and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And everything We have enumerated We have recorded in a book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *kulla* is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose explanation is *aḥṣaynāhu* (We have enumerated it). The meaning is: We enumerated everything. ﴿In a book﴾ is an emphasis on *aḥṣaynāhu*, because the meaning of *aḥṣaynāhu* and *kataknāhu* (We recorded it) is one in what is retained and established. So the meaning is: We recorded it as a book. The exegetes said: every deed was recorded by Us in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ).
﴿So taste! We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ That is, it will be said to them: taste the recompense of your deeds.

﴿Indeed, for the righteous﴾, those who did not associate partners with Allah, ﴿is a place of success﴾. On this there are two views.
One: a place of recreation. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.
Two: they succeeded by being saved from the Fire by Paradise, and from punishment by mercy. This was said by Qatada. Ibn Qutayba said: *mafāzan* is in the place of *fawz* (success).

﴿Gardens﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ḥadāʾiq* are orchards of palm trees; its singular is *ḥadīqah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and maidens of equal age﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-kawāʿib* are those with firm breasts. Ibn Fāris said: it is said, "the woman *kaʿabat* a *kaʿābah*," so she is *kāʿib*, when her breasts protrude. We have mentioned the meaning of *al-atrāb* (of equal age) in [p. 52].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾. On this there are three views.
One: it is full. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd also said so.
Two: it is continuous. This was related by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr also said so. It is also reported from Mujahid as both views.
Three: it is pure. This was said by Ikrima.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, when they drink it, ﴿any idle talk﴾, which we have mentioned in [al-Tur: 23] and elsewhere, ﴿nor any lying﴾, that is, they will not lie to one another, because the people of this world, when they drink wine, speak falsehood, but the people of Paradise are exempt from that.

Al-Farra' said: the reading of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, is *kiḍāban* with lightness, as if—and Allah knows best—they will not lie to one another therein. Al-Kisa'i would read it with lightness, and with shaddah in "They denied Our signs with complete denial (*kiddhāban*)," because "they denied" specifies *kiddhāb* as a verbal noun, whereas here it is not specified by a verb that makes it a verbal noun. We have already mentioned from Abu ʿUbayda that *kiddhāb* with shaddah and with lightness is the verbal noun of *al-mukādhaba*. Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: *kidhāb* with lightness is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, like *kitāb* is the verbal noun of *kataba*.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 78, verses 1–40 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a recompense﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that He recompensed them with that as a recompense, and likewise "a gift" (ʿaṭāʾ), because "He gave them" (aʿṭāhum) and "He recompensed them" (jāzāhum) have one meaning. And ﴿a reckoning﴾ means: what suffices them, i.e., in it is everything they desire. It is said: "Ahsabanī kadhā" (meaning "it sufficed me").

﴿Lord of the heavens﴾: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Mufaḍḍal recited "Rabbu as-samawāti wal-arḍi wa mā baynahumā al-Raḥmānu" with the bāʾ of "Rabb" and the nūn of "al-Raḥmān" in the nominative (rafʿ), meaning: He is the Lord of the heavens. ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir recited with the bāʾ and nūn in the genitive (khafḍ), as an attribute of "your Lord" (rabbika). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī recited with a kasra on the bāʾ and a rafʿ on the nūn. Al-Farrāʾ (a grammarian, the scholar who chose this reading) preferred this reading, and a group agreed with him, giving as the reason that "Rabb" is close to the genitive, while "al-Raḥmān" is further from it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not possess from Him any address﴾. There are two views concerning it:
One: they will not possess intercession except by His permission. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib. The second: creation cannot speak to the Lord except by His permission. This was said by Muqātil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾. Concerning "the Spirit" there are seven views:
The first: that it is one of the soldiers of God, the Exalted, and they are not angels. Ibn ʿAbbās related it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Mujāhid said: they are a creation in the form of the children of Adam, who eat and drink.
The second: that it is an angel greater than the heavens, the mountains and the angels. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Muqātil ibn Sulaymān. ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Spirit is an angel greater than anything God has created. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he alone stands in one row, and all the angels stand in one row, so his size is like their rows."
The third: that they are the spirits of people, who stand with the angels between the two blasts, before they are returned to the bodies. ʿAṭiyyah related it from Ibn ʿAbbās.
The fourth: that it is Jibrīl (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
The fifth: that they are the children of Adam. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.
The sixth: that it is the Qurʾān. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.
The seventh: that they are the noblest of the angels. This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the angels in rows﴾. Al-Shaʿbī said: they are two lines, one line of the Spirit and one line of the angels. On this view the meaning is: the Day the Spirit stands in rows, and the angels in rows. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿ṣaffan﴾ is "in rows" (ṣufūfan).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not speak﴾, meaning all creation, ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ to speak, ﴿and who speaks rightly﴾, i.e., who spoke rightly in the world, and this is the testimony to monotheism according to most exegetes. Mujāhid said: he spoke the truth in the world and acted upon it. ﴿That is the true Day﴾, the one that occurs and befalls without doubt. ﴿So whoever wills, let him take to his Lord a return﴾, i.e., a place of return to Him through obedience to Him.

Then He warned the disbelievers of Makkah, saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day a man will look at what his hands have put forth﴾, i.e., he will see his deed recorded in his book, whether good or bad. ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Oh, I wish I were dust!"﴾, i.e., "I wish I had not been resurrected."

Al-Thaʿlabī related from some of his teachers that he saw in some exegeses that the disbeliever here is Iblīs, because he reproached Adam, since he was created from dust, so on the Day of Resurrection he wished that he had been in the place of Adam, and said: "Oh, I wish I were dust!"

(p-3) **Surat al-Naba' (The Tidings)**
It is also called **Surat al-Tasa'ul (The Questioning)**.
It is entirely Meccan, by consensus.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ Its original form is *ʿan mā*, so the nūn was assimilated into the mīm, and the alif of *mā* was dropped, as in their saying *fīm* and *bim*. The exegetes said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, the polytheists began asking one another, saying, "What is it that he has brought?" They argued and disputed about what he had been sent with, and so this verse was revealed. The wording is that of a question, but the meaning is to magnify the matter, as they say, "What is Zayd?" when you wish to glorify his station. Then He explained what they were asking about, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿about the great tidings﴾, meaning, about the news of great importance. On this there are three views.

The first: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid, Muqatil, and al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: "When He answered, *ʿamma* became as if it meant: 'For what reason are they asking about the Qur'an?'"
The second: it is the Resurrection. This was said by Qatada.
The third: it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), related by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in which they are in disagreement﴾. For one who says it is the Qur'an, the disagreement is that the polytheists differed about it: some said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, and some said it is "the fables of the ancients," and so on. Likewise for one who says it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ). As for one who says it is the Resurrection and the Last Day, there are two views on their disagreement about it.
One: they disagreed about it when they heard of it; some of them affirmed and believed, and some denied. This is the meaning of Qatada's statement.
Two: the Muslims and the polytheists disagreed about it, the Muslims affirmed it and the polytheists denied it. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay!﴾ Some said it is a rebuke and a warning. Others said it is a negation of their disagreement, meaning: the matter is not as they say. ﴿They will come to know﴾ the outcome of their denial when the matter becomes clear. ﴿Again, nay! They will come to know﴾: a warning upon a warning. Ibn ʿAmir read *sa-ta-ʿlamūn* with the tā' in both places.

Then He mentioned His handiwork so that they might recognize His oneness, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place﴾, that is, a bed and a carpet, ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ for the earth, so that it would not sway. ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾, that is, in kinds and opposites: males and females, black and white and red. ﴿And We made your sleep a repose﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: that is, a rest for your bodies. We have explained this in [al-Furqan: 47], and we explained there His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the night a covering﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the day a means of livelihood﴾, that is, a cause of your livelihood. *Maʿāsh* means subsistence, and everything by which one lives is a *maʿāsh*. The meaning is: We made the day a time for seeking livelihood. Ibn Qutayba said: *maʿāsh* means *ʿaysh* (living), and it is a verbal noun. ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾. Muqatil said: these are the heavens, the thickness of each heaven being a five-hundred-year journey, and between every two heavens is the same distance, and they are above you, O children of Adam. So beware lest you disobey, for [they] would fall upon you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made a lamp, blazing﴾, meaning the sun. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *wahhāj* is the bright one. The philologists said: *al-Wahhāj* is the blazing one. It was also said: *al-Wahhāj* combines light and heat.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the *muʿṣirāt*﴾. On this there are three views.
One: they are the heavens. This was said by Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jubayr.
Two: they are the winds. This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Ikrima, Qatada, and Muqatil also said so. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are the south winds. According to this view, *min* means *bi* (with), so the sense is: *bi-l-muʿṣirāt* (by means of the *muʿṣirāt*). The winds were called *muʿṣirāt* because they draw out the rain.
Three: they are the clouds. This was related by al-Walibi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Rabiʿ also said so. Al-Farra' said: the cloud *muʿṣir* is one that is dripping with rain but has not yet gathered, like the girl *muʿṣir* who is almost reaching menstruation but has not yet menstruated. Ibn Qutayba likewise said: clouds were likened to young girls approaching puberty, and *muʿṣir* is a girl who has come close to menstruation. Al-Zajjaj said: the clouds were called *muʿṣirāt* just as it is said, "The crop was harvested (*ajazza*), so it is *mujazz*," meaning it reached the point of being harvested. Likewise the cloud, when it reaches the point of raining, has become *muʿṣir*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿water pouring forth﴾. Muqatil said: that is, abundant rain, poured down, each part following another. Others said: it is said *thajja al-māʾ yathujju*, when water pours out.
﴿That We may bring forth thereby﴾, that is, by that water, ﴿grain and plants﴾. On this there are two views.
One: *ḥabb* is what people eat, and *nabāt* is what the earth produces of what people and cattle eat. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zajjaj said: everything that is harvested is *ḥabb*, and everything that livestock eat of the pasture is *nabāt*.
Two: *ḥabb* is pearl and *nabāt* is grass. Ikrima said: Allah did not send down any drop from the sky without causing pearls to grow in the sea by it, and grass on the land.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and gardens, luxuriant﴾, meaning orchards. Abu ʿUbayda said: that is, intertwined with trees, with no gaps between them. The singular is *laffāʾ*, and *jannāt luff* is the plural, and the plural of the plural is *alfāf*. The exegetes said: by mentioning these created things He pointed to the Resurrection.

Two: they succeeded by being saved from the Fire by Paradise, and from punishment by mercy. This was said by Qatada. Ibn Qutayba said: *mafāzan* is in the place of *fawz* (success).

﴿Gardens﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ḥadāʾiq* are orchards of palm trees; its singular is *ḥadīqah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and maidens of equal age﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-kawāʿib* are those with firm breasts. Ibn Fāris said: it is said, "the woman *kaʿabat* a *kaʿābah*," so she is *kāʿib*, when her breasts protrude. We have mentioned the meaning of *al-atrāb* (of equal age) in [p. 52].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾. On this there are three views.
One: it is full. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd also said so.
Two: it is continuous. This was related by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr also said so. It is also reported from Mujahid as both views.
Three: it is pure. This was said by Ikrima.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, when they drink it, ﴿any idle talk﴾, which we have mentioned in [al-Tur: 23] and elsewhere, ﴿nor any lying﴾, that is, they will not lie to one another, because the people of this world, when they drink wine, speak falsehood, but the people of Paradise are exempt from that.

Al-Farra' said: the reading of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, is *kiḍāban* with lightness, as if—and Allah knows best—they will not lie to one another therein. Al-Kisa'i would read it with lightness, and with shaddah in "They denied Our signs with complete denial (*kiddhāban*)," because "they denied" specifies *kiddhāb* as a verbal noun, whereas here it is not specified by a verb that makes it a verbal noun. We have already mentioned from Abu ʿUbayda that *kiddhāb* with shaddah and with lightness is the verbal noun of *al-mukādhaba*. Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: *kidhāb* with lightness is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, like *kitāb* is the verbal noun of *kataba*.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 78, verses 1–40 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a recompense﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that He recompensed them with that as a recompense, and likewise "a gift" (ʿaṭāʾ), because "He gave them" (aʿṭāhum) and "He recompensed them" (jāzāhum) have one meaning. And ﴿a reckoning﴾ means: what suffices them, i.e., in it is everything they desire. It is said: "Ahsabanī kadhā" (meaning "it sufficed me").

﴿Lord of the heavens﴾: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Mufaḍḍal recited "Rabbu as-samawāti wal-arḍi wa mā baynahumā al-Raḥmānu" with the bāʾ of "Rabb" and the nūn of "al-Raḥmān" in the nominative (rafʿ), meaning: He is the Lord of the heavens. ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir recited with the bāʾ and nūn in the genitive (khafḍ), as an attribute of "your Lord" (rabbika). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī recited with a kasra on the bāʾ and a rafʿ on the nūn. Al-Farrāʾ (a grammarian, the scholar who chose this reading) preferred this reading, and a group agreed with him, giving as the reason that "Rabb" is close to the genitive, while "al-Raḥmān" is further from it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not possess from Him any address﴾. There are two views concerning it:
One: they will not possess intercession except by His permission. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib. The second: creation cannot speak to the Lord except by His permission. This was said by Muqātil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾. Concerning "the Spirit" there are seven views:
The first: that it is one of the soldiers of God, the Exalted, and they are not angels. Ibn ʿAbbās related it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Mujāhid said: they are a creation in the form of the children of Adam, who eat and drink.
The second: that it is an angel greater than the heavens, the mountains and the angels. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Muqātil ibn Sulaymān. ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Spirit is an angel greater than anything God has created. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he alone stands in one row, and all the angels stand in one row, so his size is like their rows."
The third: that they are the spirits of people, who stand with the angels between the two blasts, before they are returned to the bodies. ʿAṭiyyah related it from Ibn ʿAbbās.
The fourth: that it is Jibrīl (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
The fifth: that they are the children of Adam. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.
The sixth: that it is the Qurʾān. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.
The seventh: that they are the noblest of the angels. This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the angels in rows﴾. Al-Shaʿbī said: they are two lines, one line of the Spirit and one line of the angels. On this view the meaning is: the Day the Spirit stands in rows, and the angels in rows. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿ṣaffan﴾ is "in rows" (ṣufūfan).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not speak﴾, meaning all creation, ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ to speak, ﴿and who speaks rightly﴾, i.e., who spoke rightly in the world, and this is the testimony to monotheism according to most exegetes. Mujāhid said: he spoke the truth in the world and acted upon it. ﴿That is the true Day﴾, the one that occurs and befalls without doubt. ﴿So whoever wills, let him take to his Lord a return﴾, i.e., a place of return to Him through obedience to Him.

Then He warned the disbelievers of Makkah, saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day a man will look at what his hands have put forth﴾, i.e., he will see his deed recorded in his book, whether good or bad. ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Oh, I wish I were dust!"﴾, i.e., "I wish I had not been resurrected."

Al-Thaʿlabī related from some of his teachers that he saw in some exegeses that the disbeliever here is Iblīs, because he reproached Adam, since he was created from dust, so on the Day of Resurrection he wished that he had been in the place of Adam, and said: "Oh, I wish I were dust!"

(p-3) **Surat al-Naba' (The Tidings)**
It is also called **Surat al-Tasa'ul (The Questioning)**.
It is entirely Meccan, by consensus.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ Its original form is *ʿan mā*, so the nūn was assimilated into the mīm, and the alif of *mā* was dropped, as in their saying *fīm* and *bim*. The exegetes said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, the polytheists began asking one another, saying, "What is it that he has brought?" They argued and disputed about what he had been sent with, and so this verse was revealed. The wording is that of a question, but the meaning is to magnify the matter, as they say, "What is Zayd?" when you wish to glorify his station. Then He explained what they were asking about, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿about the great tidings﴾, meaning, about the news of great importance. On this there are three views.

The first: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid, Muqatil, and al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: "When He answered, *ʿamma* became as if it meant: 'For what reason are they asking about the Qur'an?'"
The second: it is the Resurrection. This was said by Qatada.
The third: it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), related by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in which they are in disagreement﴾. For one who says it is the Qur'an, the disagreement is that the polytheists differed about it: some said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, and some said it is "the fables of the ancients," and so on. Likewise for one who says it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ). As for one who says it is the Resurrection and the Last Day, there are two views on their disagreement about it.
One: they disagreed about it when they heard of it; some of them affirmed and believed, and some denied. This is the meaning of Qatada's statement.
Two: the Muslims and the polytheists disagreed about it, the Muslims affirmed it and the polytheists denied it. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay!﴾ Some said it is a rebuke and a warning. Others said it is a negation of their disagreement, meaning: the matter is not as they say. ﴿They will come to know﴾ the outcome of their denial when the matter becomes clear. ﴿Again, nay! They will come to know﴾: a warning upon a warning. Ibn ʿAmir read *sa-ta-ʿlamūn* with the tā' in both places.

Then He mentioned His handiwork so that they might recognize His oneness, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place﴾, that is, a bed and a carpet, ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ for the earth, so that it would not sway. ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾, that is, in kinds and opposites: males and females, black and white and red. ﴿And We made your sleep a repose﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: that is, a rest for your bodies. We have explained this in [al-Furqan: 47], and we explained there His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the night a covering﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the day a means of livelihood﴾, that is, a cause of your livelihood. *Maʿāsh* means subsistence, and everything by which one lives is a *maʿāsh*. The meaning is: We made the day a time for seeking livelihood. Ibn Qutayba said: *maʿāsh* means *ʿaysh* (living), and it is a verbal noun. ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾. Muqatil said: these are the heavens, the thickness of each heaven being a five-hundred-year journey, and between every two heavens is the same distance, and they are above you, O children of Adam. So beware lest you disobey, for [they] would fall upon you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made a lamp, blazing﴾, meaning the sun. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *wahhāj* is the bright one. The philologists said: *al-Wahhāj* is the blazing one. It was also said: *al-Wahhāj* combines light and heat.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the *muʿṣirāt*﴾. On this there are three views.
One: they are the heavens. This was said by Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jubayr.
Two: they are the winds. This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Ikrima, Qatada, and Muqatil also said so. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are the south winds. According to this view, *min* means *bi* (with), so the sense is: *bi-l-muʿṣirāt* (by means of the *muʿṣirāt*). The winds were called *muʿṣirāt* because they draw out the rain.
Three: they are the clouds. This was related by al-Walibi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Rabiʿ also said so. Al-Farra' said: the cloud *muʿṣir* is one that is dripping with rain but has not yet gathered, like the girl *muʿṣir* who is almost reaching menstruation but has not yet menstruated. Ibn Qutayba likewise said: clouds were likened to young girls approaching puberty, and *muʿṣir* is a girl who has come close to menstruation. Al-Zajjaj said: the clouds were called *muʿṣirāt* just as it is said, "The crop was harvested (*ajazza*), so it is *mujazz*," meaning it reached the point of being harvested. Likewise the cloud, when it reaches the point of raining, has become *muʿṣir*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿water pouring forth﴾. Muqatil said: that is, abundant rain, poured down, each part following another. Others said: it is said *thajja al-māʾ yathujju*, when water pours out.
﴿That We may bring forth thereby﴾, that is, by that water, ﴿grain and plants﴾. On this there are two views.
One: *ḥabb* is what people eat, and *nabāt* is what the earth produces of what people and cattle eat. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zajjaj said: everything that is harvested is *ḥabb*, and everything that livestock eat of the pasture is *nabāt*.
Two: *ḥabb* is pearl and *nabāt* is grass. Ikrima said: Allah did not send down any drop from the sky without causing pearls to grow in the sea by it, and grass on the land.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and gardens, luxuriant﴾, meaning orchards. Abu ʿUbayda said: that is, intertwined with trees, with no gaps between them. The singular is *laffāʾ*, and *jannāt luff* is the plural, and the plural of the plural is *alfāf*. The exegetes said: by mentioning these created things He pointed to the Resurrection.

Then He informed about the Day of Resurrection, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision﴾, that is, the Day of judgment among creatures, ﴿is an appointed time﴾ for what Allah promised of reward and punishment. ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes﴾, that is, in companies, company after company from every place. ﴿And the sky will be opened﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *wa-futtiḥat* with shaddah. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with lightness. It is opened for the descent of the angels. ﴿And it will become gates﴾, that is, having gates. ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion﴾ from their places, ﴿and they will become a mirage﴾, that is, like a mirage, because they will become scattered dust, so that the observer sees them like a mirage after their firmness and solidity. ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a place of ambush﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: *mirṣād* is a place where they lie in wait, that is, it is prepared for them, and its guardians lie in wait for the disbelievers in it. Al-Azhari said: *al-mirṣād* is the place where the watcher lies in wait for the enemy. Then He explained for whom it is an ambush, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: for the polytheists, that is, a destination.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾. Ḥamzah read *labithīn*, and the meaning in both is one. It is said: "He is *lābith* in the place" and "*labith*." Similar are *ṭāmiʿ* and *ṭamiʿ*, and *fārih* and *farih*. As for *al-aḥqāb*, it is the plural of *ḥiqb*, and we have mentioned the disagreement about it in [al-Kahf: 60].

If it is asked: what is the meaning of mentioning ages, when their dwelling in the Fire has no end? On this there are two answers.
One: this does not indicate a limit, because whenever one age passes, another follows it. Had He said "remaining therein for ten ages or five," it would have indicated a limit. This is the view of Ibn Qutayba and the majority. Its explanation is that the time of the people of Paradise and Hell can be conceived as falling under a count, even though it has no end.
Two: the meaning is that they will remain therein for ages, ﴿tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾ during the ages. As for their dwelling in the Fire, it is eternal. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Its explanation is that the ages are a limit for their punishment with boiling water and *ghassāq*; when the ages have ended, they will be punished with other punishments.
As for the meaning of *bard* (coolness), there are three views.
One: it is the coolness of drink. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: they will not taste therein the coolness of drink, nor drink.
Two: it is rest and comfort. This was said by al-Hasan and ʿAṭāʾ.
Three: it is sleep. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu ʿUbayda, and Ibn Qutayba, and they recited:
*"If I wish, I forbid women other than you, and if I wish, I do not taste cool water (nuqākh) nor sleep (bard)."*
Ibn Qutayba said: *nuqākh* is water, and *bard* is sleep, named so because the heat cools within it. Muqatil said: they will not taste therein any coolness that would benefit them from its heat, nor any drink that would benefit them from thirst. ﴿Except boiling water and *ghassāq*﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *ghasāqan* with lightness. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal, and Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim read it with shaddah.
The mention of *ḥamīm* and *ghassāq* has already preceded [p. 57].

﴿As a fitting recompense﴾. Al-Farra' said: suitable to their deeds. Others said: they are recompensed with a recompense fitting to their deeds, according to its measure. There is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾. On this there are two views.
One: they did not fear being called to account, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by the majority.
Two: they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾. Al-Farra' said: *al-kiddhāb* with shaddah is an eloquent Yemeni dialect. They say: "I denied it *kiddhāban*," and "I tore the shirt *kharrāqan*," and every *faʿaltu* in their dialect has a verbal noun with shaddah. An Arab from among them, while I was at al-Marwah, asked me for a legal ruling: "Is shaving more beloved to you, or cutting short?" And one of the Banu Kilab recited to me:
*"Indeed, it has long kept me away from my companions, and from needs whose fulfillment is my healing."*
As for the people of Najd, they say: "I denied it *takdhīban*." Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-kiddhāb* is stronger than *al-kidhāb*, and both are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual denial). Al-Aʿshā said:
*"So I believed her, and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And everything We have enumerated We have recorded in a book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *kulla* is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose explanation is *aḥṣaynāhu* (We have enumerated it). The meaning is: We enumerated everything. ﴿In a book﴾ is an emphasis on *aḥṣaynāhu*, because the meaning of *aḥṣaynāhu* and *kataknāhu* (We recorded it) is one in what is retained and established. So the meaning is: We recorded it as a book. The exegetes said: every deed was recorded by Us in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ).
﴿So taste! We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ That is, it will be said to them: taste the recompense of your deeds.

﴿Indeed, for the righteous﴾, those who did not associate partners with Allah, ﴿is a place of success﴾. On this there are two views.
One: a place of recreation. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.
Two: they succeeded by being saved from the Fire by Paradise, and from punishment by mercy. This was said by Qatada. Ibn Qutayba said: *mafāzan* is in the place of *fawz* (success).

﴿Gardens﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ḥadāʾiq* are orchards of palm trees; its singular is *ḥadīqah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and maidens of equal age﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-kawāʿib* are those with firm breasts. Ibn Fāris said: it is said, "the woman *kaʿabat* a *kaʿābah*," so she is *kāʿib*, when her breasts protrude. We have mentioned the meaning of *al-atrāb* (of equal age) in [p. 52].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾. On this there are three views.
One: it is full. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd also said so.
Two: it is continuous. This was related by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr also said so. It is also reported from Mujahid as both views.
Three: it is pure. This was said by Ikrima.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, when they drink it, ﴿any idle talk﴾, which we have mentioned in [al-Tur: 23] and elsewhere, ﴿nor any lying﴾, that is, they will not lie to one another, because the people of this world, when they drink wine, speak falsehood, but the people of Paradise are exempt from that.

Al-Farra' said: the reading of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, is *kiḍāban* with lightness, as if—and Allah knows best—they will not lie to one another therein. Al-Kisa'i would read it with lightness, and with shaddah in "They denied Our signs with complete denial (*kiddhāban*)," because "they denied" specifies *kiddhāb* as a verbal noun, whereas here it is not specified by a verb that makes it a verbal noun. We have already mentioned from Abu ʿUbayda that *kiddhāb* with shaddah and with lightness is the verbal noun of *al-mukādhaba*. Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: *kidhāb* with lightness is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, like *kitāb* is the verbal noun of *kataba*.

Al-Thaʿlabī related from some of his teachers that he saw in some exegeses that the disbeliever here is Iblīs, because he reproached Adam, since he was created from dust, so on the Day of Resurrection he wished that he had been in the place of Adam, and said: "Oh, I wish I were dust!"

(p-3) **Surat al-Naba' (The Tidings)**
It is also called **Surat al-Tasa'ul (The Questioning)**.
It is entirely Meccan, by consensus.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿About what are they asking one another?﴾ Its original form is *ʿan mā*, so the nūn was assimilated into the mīm, and the alif of *mā* was dropped, as in their saying *fīm* and *bim*. The exegetes said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, the polytheists began asking one another, saying, "What is it that he has brought?" They argued and disputed about what he had been sent with, and so this verse was revealed. The wording is that of a question, but the meaning is to magnify the matter, as they say, "What is Zayd?" when you wish to glorify his station. Then He explained what they were asking about, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿about the great tidings﴾, meaning, about the news of great importance. On this there are three views.

The first: it is the Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid, Muqatil, and al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: "When He answered, *ʿamma* became as if it meant: 'For what reason are they asking about the Qur'an?'"
The second: it is the Resurrection. This was said by Qatada.
The third: it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ), related by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿in which they are in disagreement﴾. For one who says it is the Qur'an, the disagreement is that the polytheists differed about it: some said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, and some said it is "the fables of the ancients," and so on. Likewise for one who says it is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ). As for one who says it is the Resurrection and the Last Day, there are two views on their disagreement about it.
One: they disagreed about it when they heard of it; some of them affirmed and believed, and some denied. This is the meaning of Qatada's statement.
Two: the Muslims and the polytheists disagreed about it, the Muslims affirmed it and the polytheists denied it. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay!﴾ Some said it is a rebuke and a warning. Others said it is a negation of their disagreement, meaning: the matter is not as they say. ﴿They will come to know﴾ the outcome of their denial when the matter becomes clear. ﴿Again, nay! They will come to know﴾: a warning upon a warning. Ibn ʿAmir read *sa-ta-ʿlamūn* with the tā' in both places.

Then He mentioned His handiwork so that they might recognize His oneness, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place﴾, that is, a bed and a carpet, ﴿and the mountains as pegs?﴾ for the earth, so that it would not sway. ﴿And We created you in pairs﴾, that is, in kinds and opposites: males and females, black and white and red. ﴿And We made your sleep a repose﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: that is, a rest for your bodies. We have explained this in [al-Furqan: 47], and we explained there His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the night a covering﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made the day a means of livelihood﴾, that is, a cause of your livelihood. *Maʿāsh* means subsistence, and everything by which one lives is a *maʿāsh*. The meaning is: We made the day a time for seeking livelihood. Ibn Qutayba said: *maʿāsh* means *ʿaysh* (living), and it is a verbal noun. ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾. Muqatil said: these are the heavens, the thickness of each heaven being a five-hundred-year journey, and between every two heavens is the same distance, and they are above you, O children of Adam. So beware lest you disobey, for [they] would fall upon you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We made a lamp, blazing﴾, meaning the sun. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *wahhāj* is the bright one. The philologists said: *al-Wahhāj* is the blazing one. It was also said: *al-Wahhāj* combines light and heat.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the *muʿṣirāt*﴾. On this there are three views.
One: they are the heavens. This was said by Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jubayr.
Two: they are the winds. This was related by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Ikrima, Qatada, and Muqatil also said so. Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are the south winds. According to this view, *min* means *bi* (with), so the sense is: *bi-l-muʿṣirāt* (by means of the *muʿṣirāt*). The winds were called *muʿṣirāt* because they draw out the rain.
Three: they are the clouds. This was related by al-Walibi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Dahhak, and al-Rabiʿ also said so. Al-Farra' said: the cloud *muʿṣir* is one that is dripping with rain but has not yet gathered, like the girl *muʿṣir* who is almost reaching menstruation but has not yet menstruated. Ibn Qutayba likewise said: clouds were likened to young girls approaching puberty, and *muʿṣir* is a girl who has come close to menstruation. Al-Zajjaj said: the clouds were called *muʿṣirāt* just as it is said, "The crop was harvested (*ajazza*), so it is *mujazz*," meaning it reached the point of being harvested. Likewise the cloud, when it reaches the point of raining, has become *muʿṣir*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿water pouring forth﴾. Muqatil said: that is, abundant rain, poured down, each part following another. Others said: it is said *thajja al-māʾ yathujju*, when water pours out.
﴿That We may bring forth thereby﴾, that is, by that water, ﴿grain and plants﴾. On this there are two views.
One: *ḥabb* is what people eat, and *nabāt* is what the earth produces of what people and cattle eat. This is the view of the majority. Al-Zajjaj said: everything that is harvested is *ḥabb*, and everything that livestock eat of the pasture is *nabāt*.
Two: *ḥabb* is pearl and *nabāt* is grass. Ikrima said: Allah did not send down any drop from the sky without causing pearls to grow in the sea by it, and grass on the land.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and gardens, luxuriant﴾, meaning orchards. Abu ʿUbayda said: that is, intertwined with trees, with no gaps between them. The singular is *laffāʾ*, and *jannāt luff* is the plural, and the plural of the plural is *alfāf*. The exegetes said: by mentioning these created things He pointed to the Resurrection.

Then He informed about the Day of Resurrection, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision﴾, that is, the Day of judgment among creatures, ﴿is an appointed time﴾ for what Allah promised of reward and punishment. ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes﴾, that is, in companies, company after company from every place. ﴿And the sky will be opened﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *wa-futtiḥat* with shaddah. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with lightness. It is opened for the descent of the angels. ﴿And it will become gates﴾, that is, having gates. ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion﴾ from their places, ﴿and they will become a mirage﴾, that is, like a mirage, because they will become scattered dust, so that the observer sees them like a mirage after their firmness and solidity. ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a place of ambush﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: *mirṣād* is a place where they lie in wait, that is, it is prepared for them, and its guardians lie in wait for the disbelievers in it. Al-Azhari said: *al-mirṣād* is the place where the watcher lies in wait for the enemy. Then He explained for whom it is an ambush, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for the transgressors, a place of return﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: for the polytheists, that is, a destination.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾. Ḥamzah read *labithīn*, and the meaning in both is one. It is said: "He is *lābith* in the place" and "*labith*." Similar are *ṭāmiʿ* and *ṭamiʿ*, and *fārih* and *farih*. As for *al-aḥqāb*, it is the plural of *ḥiqb*, and we have mentioned the disagreement about it in [al-Kahf: 60].

If it is asked: what is the meaning of mentioning ages, when their dwelling in the Fire has no end? On this there are two answers.
One: this does not indicate a limit, because whenever one age passes, another follows it. Had He said "remaining therein for ten ages or five," it would have indicated a limit. This is the view of Ibn Qutayba and the majority. Its explanation is that the time of the people of Paradise and Hell can be conceived as falling under a count, even though it has no end.
Two: the meaning is that they will remain therein for ages, ﴿tasting therein neither coolness nor drink﴾ during the ages. As for their dwelling in the Fire, it is eternal. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Its explanation is that the ages are a limit for their punishment with boiling water and *ghassāq*; when the ages have ended, they will be punished with other punishments.
As for the meaning of *bard* (coolness), there are three views.
One: it is the coolness of drink. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: they will not taste therein the coolness of drink, nor drink.
Two: it is rest and comfort. This was said by al-Hasan and ʿAṭāʾ.
Three: it is sleep. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu ʿUbayda, and Ibn Qutayba, and they recited:
*"If I wish, I forbid women other than you, and if I wish, I do not taste cool water (nuqākh) nor sleep (bard)."*
Ibn Qutayba said: *nuqākh* is water, and *bard* is sleep, named so because the heat cools within it. Muqatil said: they will not taste therein any coolness that would benefit them from its heat, nor any drink that would benefit them from thirst. ﴿Except boiling water and *ghassāq*﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir read *ghasāqan* with lightness. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal, and Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim read it with shaddah.
The mention of *ḥamīm* and *ghassāq* has already preceded [p. 57].

﴿As a fitting recompense﴾. Al-Farra' said: suitable to their deeds. Others said: they are recompensed with a recompense fitting to their deeds, according to its measure. There is no sin greater than polytheism, and no punishment greater than the Fire.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾. On this there are two views.
One: they did not fear being called to account, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by the majority.
Two: they did not hope for the reward of a reckoning, because they did not believe in the Resurrection. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾. Al-Farra' said: *al-kiddhāb* with shaddah is an eloquent Yemeni dialect. They say: "I denied it *kiddhāban*," and "I tore the shirt *kharrāqan*," and every *faʿaltu* in their dialect has a verbal noun with shaddah. An Arab from among them, while I was at al-Marwah, asked me for a legal ruling: "Is shaving more beloved to you, or cutting short?" And one of the Banu Kilab recited to me:
*"Indeed, it has long kept me away from my companions, and from needs whose fulfillment is my healing."*
As for the people of Najd, they say: "I denied it *takdhīban*." Abu ʿUbayda said: *al-kiddhāb* is stronger than *al-kidhāb*, and both are verbal nouns of *al-mukādhaba* (mutual denial). Al-Aʿshā said:
*"So I believed her, and I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."*

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And everything We have enumerated We have recorded in a book﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *kulla* is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose explanation is *aḥṣaynāhu* (We have enumerated it). The meaning is: We enumerated everything. ﴿In a book﴾ is an emphasis on *aḥṣaynāhu*, because the meaning of *aḥṣaynāhu* and *kataknāhu* (We recorded it) is one in what is retained and established. So the meaning is: We recorded it as a book. The exegetes said: every deed was recorded by Us in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ).
﴿So taste! We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ That is, it will be said to them: taste the recompense of your deeds.

﴿Indeed, for the righteous﴾, those who did not associate partners with Allah, ﴿is a place of success﴾. On this there are two views.
One: a place of recreation. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.
Two: they succeeded by being saved from the Fire by Paradise, and from punishment by mercy. This was said by Qatada. Ibn Qutayba said: *mafāzan* is in the place of *fawz* (success).

﴿Gardens﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-ḥadāʾiq* are orchards of palm trees; its singular is *ḥadīqah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and maidens of equal age﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *al-kawāʿib* are those with firm breasts. Ibn Fāris said: it is said, "the woman *kaʿabat* a *kaʿābah*," so she is *kāʿib*, when her breasts protrude. We have mentioned the meaning of *al-atrāb* (of equal age) in [p. 52].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾. On this there are three views.
One: it is full. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd also said so.
Two: it is continuous. This was related by Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jubayr also said so. It is also reported from Mujahid as both views.
Three: it is pure. This was said by Ikrima.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein﴾, that is, in Paradise, when they drink it, ﴿any idle talk﴾, which we have mentioned in [al-Tur: 23] and elsewhere, ﴿nor any lying﴾, that is, they will not lie to one another, because the people of this world, when they drink wine, speak falsehood, but the people of Paradise are exempt from that.

Al-Farra' said: the reading of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, is *kiḍāban* with lightness, as if—and Allah knows best—they will not lie to one another therein. Al-Kisa'i would read it with lightness, and with shaddah in "They denied Our signs with complete denial (*kiddhāban*)," because "they denied" specifies *kiddhāb* as a verbal noun, whereas here it is not specified by a verb that makes it a verbal noun. We have already mentioned from Abu ʿUbayda that *kiddhāb* with shaddah and with lightness is the verbal noun of *al-mukādhaba*. Abu ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: *kidhāb* with lightness is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, like *kitāb* is the verbal noun of *kataba*.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 78, verses 1–40 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a recompense﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that He recompensed them with that as a recompense, and likewise "a gift" (ʿaṭāʾ), because "He gave them" (aʿṭāhum) and "He recompensed them" (jāzāhum) have one meaning. And ﴿a reckoning﴾ means: what suffices them, i.e., in it is everything they desire. It is said: "Ahsabanī kadhā" (meaning "it sufficed me").

﴿Lord of the heavens﴾: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Mufaḍḍal recited "Rabbu as-samawāti wal-arḍi wa mā baynahumā al-Raḥmānu" with the bāʾ of "Rabb" and the nūn of "al-Raḥmān" in the nominative (rafʿ), meaning: He is the Lord of the heavens. ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir recited with the bāʾ and nūn in the genitive (khafḍ), as an attribute of "your Lord" (rabbika). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī recited with a kasra on the bāʾ and a rafʿ on the nūn. Al-Farrāʾ (a grammarian, the scholar who chose this reading) preferred this reading, and a group agreed with him, giving as the reason that "Rabb" is close to the genitive, while "al-Raḥmān" is further from it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not possess from Him any address﴾. There are two views concerning it:
One: they will not possess intercession except by His permission. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib. The second: creation cannot speak to the Lord except by His permission. This was said by Muqātil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾. Concerning "the Spirit" there are seven views:
The first: that it is one of the soldiers of God, the Exalted, and they are not angels. Ibn ʿAbbās related it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Mujāhid said: they are a creation in the form of the children of Adam, who eat and drink.
The second: that it is an angel greater than the heavens, the mountains and the angels. This was said by Ibn Masʿūd and Muqātil ibn Sulaymān. ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "The Spirit is an angel greater than anything God has created. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he alone stands in one row, and all the angels stand in one row, so his size is like their rows."
The third: that they are the spirits of people, who stand with the angels between the two blasts, before they are returned to the bodies. ʿAṭiyyah related it from Ibn ʿAbbās.
The fourth: that it is Jibrīl (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Shaʿbī, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.
The fifth: that they are the children of Adam. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah.
The sixth: that it is the Qurʾān. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.
The seventh: that they are the noblest of the angels. This was said by Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the angels in rows﴾. Al-Shaʿbī said: they are two lines, one line of the Spirit and one line of the angels. On this view the meaning is: the Day the Spirit stands in rows, and the angels in rows. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿ṣaffan﴾ is "in rows" (ṣufūfan).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not speak﴾, meaning all creation, ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ to speak, ﴿and who speaks rightly﴾, i.e., who spoke rightly in the world, and this is the testimony to monotheism according to most exegetes. Mujāhid said: he spoke the truth in the world and acted upon it. ﴿That is the true Day﴾, the one that occurs and befalls without doubt. ﴿So whoever wills, let him take to his Lord a return﴾, i.e., a place of return to Him through obedience to Him.

Then He warned the disbelievers of Makkah, saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Hereafter, and everything that is coming is near. ﴿The Day a man will look at what his hands have put forth﴾, i.e., he will see his deed recorded in his book, whether good or bad. ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Oh, I wish I were dust!"﴾, i.e., "I wish I had not been resurrected."

Al-Thaʿlabī related from some of his teachers that he saw in some exegeses that the disbeliever here is Iblīs, because he reproached Adam, since he was created from dust, so on the Day of Resurrection he wished that he had been in the place of Adam, and said: "Oh, I wish I were dust!"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and gardens, luxuriant﴾, meaning orchards. Abu ʿUbayda said: that is, intertwined with trees, with no gaps between them.
